answer: David's stone struck Goliath's forehead through a gap in the helmet; the giant fell; David beheaded him with his own sword
choices: David's stone struck Goliath's forehead through a gap in the helmet; the giant fell; David beheaded him with his own sword
David circled the giant and brought him down with stones at the legs; the Philistines then surrendered the field
David reasoned with Goliath and persuaded him to fall on his sword in shame before the Philistine army
David's first four stones missed; the fifth struck the heart; Goliath died standing and his army fled
context: 1 Samuel 17. Goliath's height ('six cubits and a span') is about 9'9"; some manuscripts read four cubits, still 6'9". David's victory began his rise — anointed king by Samuel in secret, became Saul's son-in-law, eventually king after Saul's death on Mount Gilboa.

question: After David's adultery with Bathsheba and arranged death of Uriah, the prophet Nathan came to the king. Rather than denounce him directly, he told a story: in a certain city lived two men, one rich with many flocks, the other poor with only one little ewe lamb that ate from his plate. A traveler came. Rather than slaughter his own sheep, the rich man took the poor man's lamb. David in fury pronounced sentence. What did Nathan then say?
answer: 'Thou art the man' — naming David himself, pronouncing the sword would never depart his house
choices: 'Thou art the man' — naming David himself, pronouncing the sword would never depart his house
'The Lord smiles' — saying David's mercy on the rich man showed a king fit to rule Israel
'Take thy lyre' — commanding David to write a psalm of restitution for the poor man's lamb
'Go and find him' — sending David personally to give the poor man a hundred lambs
context: 2 Samuel 12 records one of the most famous prophet-king confrontations in the Bible. David's instant recognition and repentance ('I have sinned against the Lord') distinguishes him from later kings who killed the prophets who confronted them. The promised judgment played out through Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah.

question: Near the end of Elijah's ministry, he and Elisha walked together from Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho to the Jordan. At each stop Elijah told Elisha to stay; Elisha refused. At the Jordan, Elijah took his mantle, smote the water, and the two crossed dry. Elijah asked what Elisha wished. Elisha asked a double portion of his spirit. Elijah said: 'If thou see me when I am taken, thou shalt have it.' As they walked, something appeared and parted them. What was it?
answer: A chariot of fire and horses of fire — and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven without tasting death
choices: A chariot of fire and horses of fire — and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven without tasting death
A column of cloud from above — Elijah ascended slowly into it while Elisha watched silently from the bank
An angel with a flaming sword — who lifted Elijah onto his back and flew north toward the cedars
A ladder of light to the throne of God — the same ladder Jacob had seen in his dream at Bethel
context: 2 Kings 2. Because he did not die, Jewish tradition expected Elijah's return before the Day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5) — at every Passover Seder a cup is set for him. Christians read John the Baptist (Matthew 11:14) as Elijah's prophetic fulfillment, with Elijah himself appearing at the Transfiguration.

question: Under Darius the Mede, Daniel — old, perhaps 80 — was one of three governors of the empire. The other two, jealous, persuaded Darius to sign an irrevocable decree: for thirty days no one might petition any god or man other than the king, on pain of being thrown to lions. Daniel prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem with windows open. The conspirators caught him. Darius could not revoke the decree. What was the morning's outcome?
answer: Daniel was found alive at dawn; God's angel had shut the lions' mouths; the conspirators and families were thrown in
choices: Daniel was found alive at dawn; God's angel had shut the lions' mouths; the conspirators and families were thrown in
Daniel emerged unharmed because the lions had refused to enter the den; the conspirators were exiled to Susa by Darius
Daniel was found dead but his body uncorrupted; Darius ordered him entombed as a saint of the Persian realm
Daniel was found preaching to the lions; they had been converted to the God of Israel by his sermon overnight
context: Daniel 6. The story prefigures Christ's resurrection in Christian typology — sealed in a stone-blocked pit, emerged alive. Daniel's lifespan from the deportation under Nebuchadnezzar (605 BC) through Cyrus places him at improbable age — his fidelity through three regimes is the point.

question: Around 587 BC, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon erected a 90-foot golden image on the plain of Dura and commanded everyone to fall down and worship when the music played. Three young Hebrew nobles — Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego — refused. Nebuchadnezzar in fury heated the furnace seven times hotter. Bound and clothed, they were thrown in; the heat killed the soldiers who threw them. Looking in, the king saw something astonishing. What?
answer: Four men walking unbound in the fire — the fourth 'like the Son of God' — and called them out unharmed
choices: Four men walking unbound in the fire — the fourth 'like the Son of God' — and called them out unharmed
The three Hebrews kneeling in flames, untouched, and an angel writing on the furnace wall in letters of fire
The three Hebrews suspended midair above the flames, surrounded by a wall of ice the fire could not melt
A pillar of fire rising from the furnace toward heaven, and the three Hebrews ascending into it like Elijah
context: Daniel 3. The 'fourth man' has been read in Christian tradition as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. The three emerged unsinged, no smell of smoke on their garments. Nebuchadnezzar promoted them and decreed that anyone speaking against the God of Israel be cut in pieces.

question: Sometime in the 8th century BC, the prophet Jonah received a commission to go to Nineveh, capital of the brutal Assyrian Empire, and preach repentance. Jonah — wanting Nineveh destroyed, not saved — boarded a ship at Joppa headed the opposite direction, to Tarshish in Spain. A great storm arose; the lot fell on Jonah; he told the sailors to throw him overboard. They did. The sea calmed. Then God prepared something. What?
answer: A great fish that swallowed Jonah whole; he spent three days and nights in its belly praying before being vomited onto land
choices: A great fish that swallowed Jonah whole; he spent three days and nights in its belly praying before being vomited onto land
An island that rose from the deep beneath him; he lived there forty days before a Phoenician ship rescued him
A pillar of cloud that bore him through the air across the Mediterranean to the gates of Nineveh in a single night
A sea-cave to which a porpoise carried him; he emerged three days later having debated the spirit of Leviathan
context: Jonah 1-2. Jesus invoked it as 'the sign of Jonah' — three days in the belly of the deep prefiguring his own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:40). Jonah did eventually preach; the city repented from king to cattle; Jonah sulked under a withered gourd, angry at God's mercy.

question: Near the end of the wilderness wandering, with Miriam newly dead and the people again complaining of thirst at Kadesh, God commanded Moses and Aaron to take Aaron's rod, speak to the rock before the assembly, and water would come. Moses, in fury at the people, struck the rock twice with the rod, saying 'must we fetch you water out of this rock?' Water gushed; the people drank. But God pronounced judgment on Moses and Aaron. What was it?
answer: Because they did not sanctify him before the people, neither would lead the congregation into the promised land
choices: Because they did not sanctify him before the people, neither would lead the congregation into the promised land
Because they had stolen God's glory by saying 'must WE fetch water,' their rods would turn to serpents at sunset
Because Moses had struck rather than spoken, the rod itself would burst into flame and consume him at midnight
Because they had borne false witness by calling the people rebels, their tents would be moved outside the camp
context: Numbers 20 records the incident at Meribah. Moses saw the promised land from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34) but never entered. The judgment troubled later commentators; midrash and Christian readings see it as the standard to which God holds his greatest servants. Moses died at 120; the people mourned thirty days.

question: Around 950 BC, hearing of Solomon's wisdom, a queen traveled from a kingdom in southwestern Arabia (or perhaps Ethiopia) to Jerusalem with a great train: camels of spices, gold, and precious stones. She tested Solomon with hard questions. He answered all. She saw the wisdom of Solomon, the house, the meat of his table, the sitting of his servants, his ascent to the Temple. What did she say?
answer: 'The half was not told me; thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard' — and gave him 120 talents of gold
choices: 'The half was not told me; thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard' — and gave him 120 talents of gold
'Thy God hath chosen poorly; an Arabian king would not bear such taxation' — and returned to Sheba with the spices
'I came in pride and depart in shame; deliver me from my idols' — and was baptized in the priestly laver of the Temple
'Thy father David was greater than thee in poverty' — and went up to David's tomb to offer her gifts there
context: 1 Kings 10. The Queen of Sheba (Makeda in Ethiopian tradition, Bilqis in Arabic) gave Solomon 120 talents of gold — perhaps 4 tonnes. Ethiopian tradition holds she bore him a son, Menelik I, founding the Solomonic dynasty that ruled Ethiopia until Haile Selassie's deposition in 1974.

question: After the Magi failed to return to him, Herod the Great — an aging tyrant who had executed his own wife Mariamne and three of his sons — was wroth. Warned in a dream, Joseph had already taken Mary and the child to Egypt. Herod, calculating from the date the Magi told him of the star, ordered an act that Matthew says fulfilled Jeremiah 31:15 ('Rachel weeping for her children'). What did he order?
answer: The killing of all male children in Bethlehem and its borders, two years old and under — perhaps 20-30 toddlers
choices: The killing of all male children in Bethlehem and its borders, two years old and under — perhaps 20-30 toddlers
The burning of every house in Bethlehem and forced exile of the inhabitants to the Nabatean kingdom
The execution of every firstborn son in Jerusalem itself — a reverse Passover targeting the heir of David
The crucifixion of every Hebrew priest serving in the Temple that month for failing to identify the child
context: Matthew 2:16-18. Bethlehem was a small village (likely 300-1,000 people), so the death toll was likely small — but the act was characteristic of Herod's last years. The Catholic feast of the Holy Innocents falls December 28; they are venerated as the first Christian martyrs.

question: Around 28 or 29 AD, in the wilderness of Judea near the Jordan River, John the Baptist was baptizing those who came confessing their sins, preaching 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' Jesus, then about thirty, came from Galilee to be baptized. John tried to refuse — 'I have need to be baptized of thee.' Jesus answered 'suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness.' He was baptized. What happened as he came up?
answer: The heavens opened, the Spirit of God descended like a dove, and a voice from heaven said 'This is my beloved Son'
choices: The heavens opened, the Spirit of God descended like a dove, and a voice from heaven said 'This is my beloved Son'
A great wind from the desert filled the Jordan valley and the river ceased flowing for the space of an hour
The Jordan turned to blood for a single instant, then back to water, and the people fled in fear of judgment
A pillar of cloud descended and overshadowed Jesus, John, and the whole baptismal site until the evening
context: Matthew 3, Mark 1, Luke 3, and John 1 all record the baptism — one of the few episodes in all four Gospels. The descent of the Spirit and the voice from heaven mark Jesus's commissioning. The Trinitarian shape (Father speaking, Son baptized, Spirit descending) was foundational for later Trinitarian theology.

question: Immediately after his baptism, the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness where he fasted forty days. At the end he was hungry. The tempter approached with three temptations. First: turn stones to bread; Jesus refused, citing Deuteronomy 8. Second: throw himself from the Temple pinnacle; Jesus refused, citing Deuteronomy 6. The third took him to a high mountain. What did the tempter offer?
answer: 'All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me' — to which Jesus replied 'Get thee hence, Satan'
choices: 'All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me' — to which Jesus replied 'Get thee hence, Satan'
'All these crowns will I give thee, if thou shouldst fast forty more days' — to which Jesus replied with silence only
'All this gold will I give thee, if thou shalt enter the priesthood at Jerusalem' — to which Jesus replied with weeping
'All these armies will I give thee, if thou shalt overthrow the Roman Empire' — to which Jesus replied with fasting
context: Matthew 4 and Luke 4. Each invitation tested a different prerogative — provision, providence, power. Jesus's threefold scriptural reply (all from Deuteronomy) set a pattern for Christian resistance to temptation: not argument but Scripture. Mark 1:13 mentions wild beasts and angels.

question: About six days after Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up into a high mountain (traditionally Mount Tabor). He was transfigured — face shining as the sun, garments white as light. Two figures appeared talking with him. Peter, terrified, suggested building three tabernacles. A bright cloud overshadowed them and a voice came from the cloud. Who were the two figures, and what did the voice say?
answer: Moses and Elijah — and the voice said 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him'
choices: Moses and Elijah — and the voice said 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him'
Abraham and David — and the voice said 'These are my chosen witnesses to my chosen Son; receive him now'
Adam and Noah — and the voice said 'The first man and the new man are made one in this beloved Son'
Isaiah and Ezekiel — and the voice said 'The prophets are fulfilled; the Word is made flesh; behold him'
context: Matthew 17, Mark 9, Luke 9 all record the Transfiguration. Moses (Law) and Elijah (Prophets) together attest the Christ. Luke adds that they spoke of his 'exodus' he would accomplish at Jerusalem. Eastern Orthodoxy gives the feast central importance (August 6).

question: The Sunday before Passover, around 30 or 33 AD, Jesus approached Jerusalem from Bethphage on the Mount of Olives. He sent two disciples for an ass colt 'whereon yet never man sat,' fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. The disciples set their garments on the colt and Jesus rode toward the city. A great multitude spread their garments and cut palm branches, strewing them in the way and crying. What did the crowd cry?
answer: 'Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord' — and the city was moved
choices: 'Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord' — and the city was moved
'Caesar is fallen, the Messiah reigneth' — directly challenging Roman authority before Pilate's residence
'Burn the Temple, raise the new' — anticipating the destruction of 70 AD prophesied that same week
'Slay the high priest, anoint the new' — addressing the Sadducean Temple aristocracy by name in public
context: All four Gospels record the entry. Palm branches were symbols of victory and national liberation (used at the Feast of Tabernacles and the Maccabean re-dedication of the Temple). The crowd expected a Davidic king to expel Rome; Jesus rode a donkey of peace. By Friday the same crowd cried 'Crucify him.'

question: On Thursday evening of Passion Week — the start of Passover by Synoptic reckoning — Jesus gathered the twelve in an upper room in Jerusalem (traditionally the Cenacle on Mount Zion). They reclined at table. He took bread, blessed and broke it, gave to them: 'Take, eat; this is my body.' He took the cup, gave thanks, gave to them, saying — what?
answer: 'Drink ye all of it; for this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins'
choices: 'Drink ye all of it; for this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins'
'Pour ye all of it; for this is the wine of the kingdom, which we shall drink anew in the Father's house above'
'Bless ye all of it; for this is the cup of the prophets, sealed by the elders of Israel from of old by the law'
'Hold ye all of it; for this is the libation of the saints, offered with the spices of the morning sacrifice'
context: Matthew 26, Mark 14, Luke 22, and 1 Corinthians 11 all record the institution. The four traditions differ in detail — 'new covenant' language is strongest in Luke and Paul. The Eucharist became the central act of Christian worship; the question of how Christ is present divided Catholics, Lutherans, Reformed, and Anglicans at the Reformation.

question: After the trial, Jesus was scourged, mocked with a crown of thorns and purple robe, led out to Golgotha ('place of a skull,' Latinized Calvary) outside Jerusalem's walls. Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry the crossbeam. Two others were crucified with him. The Roman superscription over his head was in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. What did it say, and who were the two with him?
answer: 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews' (INRI) — and they were two thieves (robbers / brigands), one right and one left
choices: 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews' (INRI) — and they were two thieves (robbers / brigands), one right and one left
'Jesus the Heretic, King of Beasts' — and they were two priests of the Temple, accused of profaning the holy place
'Jesus, Son of Joseph the Carpenter' — and they were two slaves of Pilate, accused of stealing the prefect's seal
'Jesus of Galilee, Friend of Sinners' — and they were two zealots, captured during the cleansing of the Temple
context: John 19 records the trilingual superscription — the priests protested but Pilate would not alter it. Luke 23 records the dialogue between the thieves and Jesus: one mocked, the other repented ('Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom'). Jesus's reply: 'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.'

question: As Jesus hung from the sixth hour (noon) until the ninth (3 PM), darkness covered the land. When he cried with a loud voice and yielded up the ghost, the veil of the Temple was rent in twain top to bottom; the earth quaked; rocks split; tombs opened. The Roman centurion who stood facing him — the officer in charge of the execution party, who had seen many crucifixions — was watching. What did he say?
answer: 'Truly this was the Son of God' (Matthew) / 'Certainly this was a righteous man' (Luke) — a Roman professional's testimony
choices: 'Truly this was the Son of God' (Matthew) / 'Certainly this was a righteous man' (Luke) — a Roman professional's testimony
'I have crucified a god of the Hebrews; my hand shall not hold the sword again until I be cleansed' — and he resigned
'Caesar must hear of this; this man was no rebel' — and he reported to Pilate the same evening of these signs
'Hosanna in the highest' — the Gentile centurion taking up the Palm Sunday cry of the Jewish crowd from the week before
context: Matthew 27:54, Mark 15:39, Luke 23:47 all record the confession. Mark, addressing a Roman audience, places it at the climax of his Gospel — the first human confession of Jesus as 'Son of God' on the Roman model (where Caesar bore that title). Tradition gives the centurion the name Longinus.

question: On the first day of the week, very early, while it was yet dark, certain women — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, Salome, Joanna, depending on the Gospel — came to the tomb bringing spices to anoint the body. The tomb was a new one belonging to Joseph of Arimathea, hewn from rock, with a great stone rolled before the door, sealed and guarded. They wondered who would roll away the stone. What did they find?
answer: The stone rolled away and the tomb empty — and an angel (or two men in shining garments) saying 'He is not here, but is risen'
choices: The stone rolled away and the tomb empty — and an angel (or two men in shining garments) saying 'He is not here, but is risen'
The guards alive but paralyzed in fear — and the body of Jesus standing untouched beside the open tomb door
The tomb sealed but empty within — and the spices uncorrupted in the linen wrappings on the slab as a sign
The stone in place but warm to touch — and the angel calling them to wait three more days for the resurrection
context: All four Gospels record the empty tomb. The angelic announcement — 'He is not here; he is risen, as he said' — became the founding confession. Pauline tradition (1 Corinthians 15) lists the appearances: to Peter, the Twelve, more than 500 brethren at once, James, Paul himself.

question: Forty days after the Resurrection, Jesus led the disciples out as far as Bethany on the Mount of Olives. He had spent the intervening time appearing to them, opening the scriptures, eating with them, and commissioning them. He told them to remain in Jerusalem until they were endued with power from on high. He blessed them, and was parted from them. What is the description of his departure?
answer: He was taken up; a cloud received him out of their sight; two men in white said 'this same Jesus shall so come in like manner'
choices: He was taken up; a cloud received him out of their sight; two men in white said 'this same Jesus shall so come in like manner'
He was transfigured before them and faded into pure light; the disciples fell on their faces; a voice said 'wait yet a while'
He walked out into the desert beyond Bethany; they followed at a distance until they could see him no more in the dust
He stepped onto a chariot of fire as Elijah had done; the disciples watched it rise over the eastern horizon at noon
context: Acts 1:9-11, Luke 24:50-51, Mark 16:19 all record the Ascension. The Feast of the Ascension falls forty days after Easter, traditionally a Thursday. The promise undergirds Christian eschatology. The Mount of Olives is the place from which Zechariah 14 prophesies the return.

question: Matthew 5-7 records the Sermon on the Mount — Jesus's longest discourse, given on a hillside near Capernaum. It opens with the Beatitudes ('Blessed are the poor in spirit...'), continues through teaching on the law ('I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil'), the antitheses ('Ye have heard... but I say unto you'), the Lord's Prayer, treasures in heaven, judging others, and the wise and foolish builders. Which of the following is NOT from the Sermon on the Mount?
answer: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me'
choices: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me'
'Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?'
'Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment'
'Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself'
context: The 'I am the way' saying is from John 14:6 (Last Supper discourse). The Sermon on the Mount is foundational for Christian ethics — Tolstoy built a pacifist philosophy on it; Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937) anchors itself in it; Gandhi reportedly read it daily despite remaining Hindu.

question: The Sermon on the Mount opens with eight (or nine) Beatitudes — sayings that begin 'Blessed are...' and pronounce divine favor on unexpected qualities or conditions. Each pairs a present blessing with a future promise. Which of the following is NOT one of the Beatitudes as recorded in Matthew 5?
answer: 'Blessed are the rich: for they shall inherit the kingdom of righteousness'
choices: 'Blessed are the rich: for they shall inherit the kingdom of righteousness'
'Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth'
'Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God'
'Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God'
context: The Beatitudes invert worldly expectations — favor falls on the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, those persecuted for righteousness. Luke's Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6) adds woes — 'Woe unto you that are rich' — making the inversion explicit.

question: In Matthew 25, the final discourse before the Passion, Jesus pictured the Last Judgment. The Son of man shall come in his glory, sit on his throne; all nations gathered; he separates them as a shepherd divides sheep from goats. To the sheep on his right he says 'come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world.' Why?
answer: 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat; thirsty, ye gave me drink; a stranger, ye took me in; naked, ye clothed me'
choices: 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat; thirsty, ye gave me drink; a stranger, ye took me in; naked, ye clothed me'
'Ye observed the sabbath of the Lord; ye paid the tithe of mint and rue; ye fasted the prescribed fasts of the elders'
'Ye believed without seeing; ye confessed me before kings; ye kept the doctrines of the apostles pure of all error'
'Ye crucified the flesh with the affections; ye left house and lands for my name; ye took up the cross daily'
context: Matthew 25:31-46 ends the synoptic ministry with the sheep and goats — judgment based on treatment of the hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, imprisoned. 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' Catholic Worker movement, liberation theology, evangelical mercy ministries all draw from it.

question: Matthew's Gospel ends on a mountain in Galilee, after the Resurrection, where Jesus had appointed the eleven to meet him. They worshipped him; some doubted. He came and spoke to them, claiming a comprehensive authority and commissioning the disciples with their permanent task. What is the Great Commission as recorded in Matthew 28:18-20?
answer: 'All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them... teaching them to observe all things'
choices: 'All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them... teaching them to observe all things'
'Tarry in Jerusalem until ye be endued with power from on high. Go not until the comforter come; he shall guide you into all truth'
'I appoint a kingdom unto you, as my Father hath appointed unto me. Ye shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel'
'I send the promise of my Father upon you. Behold, the angels shall ascend and descend upon the Son of man from henceforth'
context: The Great Commission has been the charter for Christian missions for two millennia. The Trinitarian baptismal formula ('in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost') is among the earliest Trinitarian formulas in the New Testament. The closing words — 'lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world' — are the last words of Matthew's Gospel.

question: Soon after Pentecost, the apostles appointed seven deacons to handle daily distribution to widows. Among them was Stephen — full of faith, doing great wonders. The Synagogue of the Freedmen disputed with him but could not resist his wisdom. They suborned witnesses and dragged him before the Sanhedrin. His defense (Acts 7) was a sweeping review of Hebrew history ending in a vision. What happened?
answer: He cried 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God' — they stoned him to death
choices: He cried 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God' — they stoned him to death
He was acquitted by Gamaliel's reasoning, released, and martyred a year later by a Sicarii dagger in the Temple courts
He died of his wounds in prison three days later, having converted his jailer and the jailer's whole household
He was banished to Cyrene where he was crucified upside down by Roman authorities at the request of the Sanhedrin
context: Acts 7-8 records Stephen as the first Christian martyr (c. 34 AD). The young Saul (later Paul) consented to his death and held the coats of the witnesses. Stephen's prayer — 'Lord, lay not this sin to their charge' — echoed Jesus's words from the cross. His feast falls December 26 in Western Christianity.

question: Around 34 AD, Saul of Tarsus — a Pharisee, student of Gamaliel, zealous persecutor of the new Christian movement — obtained letters from the high priest authorizing him to arrest any followers of the Way he could find in Damascus. As he traveled, near noon, a great light from heaven suddenly shone around him. He fell to the earth and heard a voice. What did it say, and what was the immediate result?
answer: 'Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? I am Jesus.' Saul rose blind; his companions led him by hand to Damascus to fast three days
choices: 'Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? I am Jesus.' Saul rose blind; his companions led him by hand to Damascus to fast three days
'Saul, Saul, come unto me.' Saul rose with a tongue of fire on his head; his companions saw it and fled into the desert
'Saul, Saul, behold thy crown.' Saul rose with a scroll in his hand; he wandered alone three days reading it in silence
'Saul, Saul, take up thy cross.' Saul rose carrying a wooden beam; his companions abandoned him on the dusty road
context: Acts 9, 22, 26 all record the Damascus road conversion. Ananias was sent to lay hands on Saul; scales fell from his eyes; he was baptized. Saul (Paul after his mission to the Gentiles) became the apostle to the nations, author of thirteen New Testament letters, the most influential theologian of the first generation.

question: Around 50 AD, during his second missionary journey, Paul came to Athens — the intellectual capital of the ancient world. While waiting for Silas and Timothy, his spirit was stirred by seeing the city wholly given to idolatry. He disputed in the synagogue and in the agora daily. Epicureans and Stoics encountered him; some called him a babbler. They brought him to the Areopagus (Mars Hill) for a hearing. What did he do as he began his address?
answer: Quoted an inscription he had seen — 'TO THE UNKNOWN GOD' — and proclaimed that God was the one they ignorantly worshipped
choices: Quoted an inscription he had seen — 'TO THE UNKNOWN GOD' — and proclaimed that God was the one they ignorantly worshipped
Called fire from heaven onto the altar of Athena and demolished the statue of Zeus standing nearby on the rock
Spoke Aristotle's Greek tongue with such grace that Plato's heirs offered him a chair in the Academy on the spot
Cursed the Athenian gods one by one by name until the Areopagus court forbade him to speak any further
context: Acts 17 records the Areopagus sermon — Paul citing the Greek poets (Aratus's Phaenomena) and reasoning toward the resurrection. Some mocked, some said 'we will hear thee again,' some believed — including Dionysius the Areopagite. The episode is a model for Christian engagement with non-Christian thought.

question: Paul's missionary career spanned roughly 47-58 AD across three documented journeys recorded in Acts. The first (47-49) covered Cyprus, southern Anatolia. The second (49-52) extended to Macedonia and Greece. The third (53-58) consolidated work in Asia Minor and Greece. Each journey ended with Paul returning to a particular city. Which city was Paul's primary base — the church that commissioned him, to which he returned between journeys?
answer: Antioch in Syria — where disciples were first called Christians and where the missionary commission originated
choices: Antioch in Syria — where disciples were first called Christians and where the missionary commission originated
Tarsus in Cilicia — Paul's hometown where he had been a tentmaker before his Damascus road conversion
Caesarea Maritima — the Roman administrative capital on the coast where Cornelius the centurion had been baptized
Jerusalem — the original Christian center where the apostles continued to gather for the major decisions
context: Acts 11:26 places the disciples' first being called Christians at Antioch. Acts 13:2 records the commissioning of Barnabas and Saul there by the Spirit. Antioch — now Antakya, Turkey — was the third-largest city in the Roman Empire and became the launchpad for the gentile mission. Each journey began and ended with reports there.

question: After two years of house arrest in Rome (Acts ends here, c. 62 AD), Paul was likely released, made further journeys (possibly to Spain), and was rearrested. Tradition holds he was beheaded outside Rome during Nero's persecution following the great fire of 64 AD — which Nero blamed on Christians. Peter, also in Rome by tradition, met a different fate. According to early Christian tradition, what was Peter's execution?
answer: Crucified upside down — Peter requesting it, considering himself unworthy to die in the same posture as his Lord
choices: Crucified upside down — Peter requesting it, considering himself unworthy to die in the same posture as his Lord
Burned at the stake in Nero's gardens — alongside the Christians Tacitus describes as covered in pitch and set alight
Beheaded with Paul on the same day, the same sword — June 29 according to Roman martyrology
Stoned to death by a Roman crowd — having denied the imperial cult in the Forum before Nero himself
context: Eusebius (4th century) records the inverted crucifixion tradition. Both apostles are traditionally commemorated June 29. Tacitus's Annals 15.44 describes Nero's persecution after the fire: Christians 'covered with the skins of beasts, were torn by dogs and perished, or were nailed to crosses, or were doomed to the flames.'

question: Around 50 AD, a major crisis hit the early church: must Gentile converts be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to be Christians? Some from Judea taught yes. Paul and Barnabas disputed. The matter was referred to Jerusalem. Peter recalled his vision of clean and unclean animals; James (brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church) gave the decisive judgment. What did the Council of Jerusalem decree?
answer: Gentile converts need not be circumcised — only abstain from idol-meat, blood, things strangled, and fornication
choices: Gentile converts need not be circumcised — only abstain from idol-meat, blood, things strangled, and fornication
All Gentile converts must be circumcised by their first Passover after conversion — the only law required to remain
Gentile churches must keep all 613 commandments of the Mosaic Law within three generations of conversion
Only Gentile males in Jerusalem must be circumcised — those abroad were exempt by the diaspora privilege
context: Acts 15 records the Jerusalem Council — arguably the most consequential meeting in Christian history. The four restrictions (the 'Apostolic Decree') reflect concern for table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile Christians. Paul's letter to the Galatians, possibly contemporaneous, presents the issue with greater theological force: justification by faith, not by works of the law.

question: Around 155 AD, Polycarp — bishop of Smyrna, said to have been a disciple of the apostle John himself — was arrested during a wave of persecution. He was about 86. Brought before the proconsul in the stadium, he was urged to swear by the genius of Caesar, curse Christ, and be released. The proconsul threatened him with wild beasts, then with fire. What was Polycarp's famous reply?
answer: 'Eighty and six years have I served him, and he hath done me no wrong: how can I blaspheme my King who saved me?'
choices: 'Eighty and six years have I served him, and he hath done me no wrong: how can I blaspheme my King who saved me?'
'I am old and my voice fails: send me wild beasts that they may hasten what years have left undone in me'
'Thy fire is cold compared to the eternal fire prepared for the wicked: cast me in and I shall feel no warmth'
'Thy Caesar reigneth but a season: my King reigneth forever in the heavens far above the realm of Rome'
context: The Martyrdom of Polycarp (c. 155) is the earliest extra-biblical Christian martyrdom account preserved in full. The proconsul ordered him burned; the flames reportedly formed an arch around him; a soldier was sent to stab him with a dagger. Polycarp links the apostolic generation to the second-century church — a direct chain back to John.

question: Athanasius (c. 296-373) was bishop of Alexandria from 328 until his death — except for the five exiles totaling 17 years that emperors imposed on him for his refusal to compromise the Nicene faith. Throughout this period, Arian or semi-Arian emperors held the imperial throne; most bishops capitulated. Athanasius did not. A famous Latin phrase summarizes his career. What is it?
answer: Athanasius contra mundum — Athanasius against the world — celebrating his lonely stand for orthodoxy
choices: Athanasius contra mundum — Athanasius against the world — celebrating his lonely stand for orthodoxy
Athanasius pro Deo — Athanasius for God — emphasizing his theological positivity rather than opposition
Athanasius Patriarcha — Athanasius the Patriarch — emphasizing his episcopal authority over Egypt
Athanasius semper victor — Athanasius ever victorious — emphasizing his eventual triumph at councils
context: Athanasius's 'On the Incarnation' (c. 318) remains the classic statement of why God became man. His Festal Letter of 367 is the first list to enumerate exactly the 27 books of the New Testament canon as we have them. His persistence is widely credited with preserving Nicene orthodoxy through fifty years of Arian imperial pressure.

question: Augustine of Hippo (354-430) is the most influential theologian in Western Christianity. Born in Thagaste in Roman North Africa to a pagan father and Christian mother Monica, he received a classical education. As a young man he abandoned Christianity for Manichaeism for nine years; he took a concubine and had a son. He moved to Milan as imperial rhetor in 384. There he encountered an exceptional bishop. Who?
answer: Ambrose of Milan — whose preaching dissolved Augustine's Manichaean objections and prepared his Christian conversion
choices: Ambrose of Milan — whose preaching dissolved Augustine's Manichaean objections and prepared his Christian conversion
Jerome of Bethlehem — translator of the Vulgate, who happened to be passing through on a mission to consult the imperial court
Hilary of Poitiers — bishop and theologian who personally received Augustine into the catechumenate before his conversion
Damasus of Rome — the pope who commissioned the Vulgate and welcomed Augustine to Rome for instruction in the faith
context: Ambrose (c. 339-397) — provincial governor turned bishop by popular acclamation — was the preacher whose teaching dissolved Augustine's Manichaean objections to Genesis. Ambrose baptized Augustine at the Easter vigil 387. The Latin hymns Ambrose wrote (Te Deum etc.) shaped Western liturgy; his confrontations with the emperor Theodosius established a principle of ecclesiastical independence from imperial power.

question: In August 386 AD, Augustine was 31, imperial rhetor in Milan, tormented by his inability to break from concubinage despite intellectual conviction of Christian truth. In the garden of his lodging, he flung himself under a fig tree weeping. He heard a child's voice chanting 'tolle lege' — 'take up and read.' Taking it as divine command, he opened Paul's letters at random. What did he read?
answer: Romans 13:13-14 — 'not in chambering and wantonness... but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ' — and the doubt was resolved
choices: Romans 13:13-14 — 'not in chambering and wantonness... but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ' — and the doubt was resolved
Galatians 5:22 — the fruits of the Spirit — and he immediately began a new ascetic life of teaching and prayer
1 Corinthians 13 — the love chapter — and he wept over his lost years before turning to compose hymns to charity
Philippians 4:13 — 'I can do all things through Christ' — and he rose to his feet healed of his sexual compulsions
context: Augustine recounts the garden conversion in Confessions Book 8 — one of the foundational texts of Western autobiography. The 'tolle lege' moment is among the most-painted scenes in Christian art. Augustine was baptized by Ambrose the following Easter vigil (April 24-25, 387). His mother Monica died at Ostia later that year, content that her prayers were answered.

question: In April 1204, the army of the Fourth Crusade — diverted from its planned attack on Muslim Egypt — sacked Constantinople, the capital of Byzantine (Eastern Christian) civilization. The crusaders had been bankrolled by Venice; the doge Enrico Dandolo (over 90, blind) led the assault. The city was looted for three days. Holy relics were carried west. What was the lasting consequence for Christian unity?
answer: Permanent rupture between Catholic and Orthodox churches — the Great Schism of 1054 was now sealed in blood
choices: Permanent rupture between Catholic and Orthodox churches — the Great Schism of 1054 was now sealed in blood
Restoration of Christian unity — Orthodox patriarch acknowledged Roman primacy as a result of military defeat
Conversion of Russia to Catholicism — the Russian church transferred allegiance from Constantinople to Rome
Unification of all eastern Christianity under a single Latin patriarch ruling from Constantinople for 60 years
context: The 1204 sack of Constantinople deepened the 1054 schism beyond healing — Orthodox Christians have never forgotten it. The Latin Empire of Constantinople (1204-1261) ruled from the looted city until the Byzantines recovered it. Many of the great works of art (the Horses of San Marco, the Pala d'Oro) and relics now in Venice came from the sack.

question: Julian of Norwich (c. 1343-after 1416) was an English anchoress — a woman enclosed for life in a cell attached to a church. In May 1373, at age 30, she received a series of sixteen visions (or 'showings') during a near-fatal illness. She wrote a short account immediately; she later expanded a fuller text after twenty years of contemplation. Her Revelations of Divine Love is the first known book in English written by a woman. What is her most famous phrase?
answer: 'All shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — Christ's reassurance to her in the visions
choices: 'All shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — Christ's reassurance to her in the visions
'Love is patient, love is kind' — a phrase she actually adapted from 1 Corinthians 13 with attribution
'Now I shall be all in love' — her dying words recorded by her companion at the anchorhold
'In Christ I find my life' — her abridged life-motto inscribed on the wall of her Norwich cell
context: T. S. Eliot quoted 'all shall be well' in 'Little Gidding' (Four Quartets, 1942). Julian's striking image of Christ as Mother and her theology of the never-failing love of God have made her unusually appealing to modern readers. Her anchorhold survives at the Church of St. Julian, Norwich (rebuilt after WWII bombing); pilgrims visit regularly.

question: Meister Eckhart (c. 1260-1328) was a German Dominican preacher and mystical theologian whose vernacular sermons in Middle High German made him one of the most original voices in medieval Christianity. He preached on detachment (Abgeschiedenheit), the birth of the Word in the soul, and the depths of the Godhead. Some of his statements alarmed church authorities; he was posthumously condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329. Of what was he accused?
answer: Pantheism — apparently dissolving the Creator-creature distinction in language about the soul's union with God
choices: Pantheism — apparently dissolving the Creator-creature distinction in language about the soul's union with God
Pelagianism — denying the necessity of grace by emphasizing the soul's natural capacity for divine union
Donatism — denying the validity of sacraments performed by unworthy priests in his German diocese
Iconoclasm — denying the legitimacy of religious images, particularly in the Frankfurt Dominican houses
context: Eckhart's bold language — 'the eye with which I see God is the eye with which God sees me' — was vulnerable to misinterpretation. His defenders argue he was misunderstood; modern scholarship has largely rehabilitated him. He influenced the German mystics Tauler and Suso, the Theologia Germanica (later quoted by Luther), and modern interpreters from Schopenhauer to Heidegger.

question: On July 6, 1415, the Czech priest Jan Hus — rector of Charles University in Prague, preacher in the Bethlehem Chapel, critic of Church abuses — was burned at Constance. Emperor Sigismund had promised safe conduct. Hus had drawn on John Wycliffe's earlier teachings against indulgences and clerical wealth. What movement did his death ignite?
answer: The Hussite Wars (1419-1434) — Czech Hussite armies, led by Jan Žižka, repeatedly defeated imperial crusades sent against them
choices: The Hussite Wars (1419-1434) — Czech Hussite armies, led by Jan Žižka, repeatedly defeated imperial crusades sent against them
The First Lutheran Crusade — a unified German Protestant response that proved decades premature and was crushed quickly
The Catholic Counter-Reformation — Trent's reforms were initiated in direct response to Hus's death within the same year
The Jesuit Order — Ignatius of Loyola founded the order specifically to counter the Hussite legacy in Eastern Europe
context: Hus's death (despite Sigismund's safe-conduct, which the council ruled void for heretics) outraged Bohemia. The Hussite Wars saw Jan Žižka's wagenburg tactics defeat five papal crusades. The Compactata of 1436 gave Bohemia communion in both kinds (bread and wine for laity) and tolerated some Hussite practices. Luther later said 'We are all Hussites without knowing it.'

question: On April 17-18, 1521, at the Diet of Worms, Emperor Charles V demanded that Martin Luther — who had now been excommunicated by Pope Leo X (Decet Romanum Pontificem, January 1521) — recant his teachings. A pile of his books lay on a table. Luther asked for one day to consider. The next day, he refused. According to the most famous version of his words, what did he say?
answer: 'Here I stand, I can do no other; my conscience is captive to the Word of God; to act against conscience is neither right nor safe'
choices: 'Here I stand, I can do no other; my conscience is captive to the Word of God; to act against conscience is neither right nor safe'
'I will not recant, for the Pope is the Antichrist, and the Antichrist's authority can compel no Christian conscience'
'My books shall remain unburned, for they testify to the truth of Christ against the false church of indulgences'
'I appeal to the next general council, which alone has authority to judge between me and the bishop of Rome'
context: Modern scholarship doubts the precise 'Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders' formulation appeared in the original 1521 records — but Luther did refuse to recant unless convinced by scripture or evident reason. Charles V issued the Edict of Worms (May 25, 1521) declaring Luther an outlaw. Luther's protector Elector Frederick the Wise had him spirited away to Wartburg Castle for safety.

question: In 1524-1525, German peasants in southern and central Germany rose in armed revolt — the Peasants' War, the largest popular uprising in Europe before the French Revolution. Their Twelve Articles drew on Luther's language of Christian freedom, demanding social reforms. Perhaps 100,000 peasants died. Luther's response shocked many sympathizers. What did he write?
answer: 'Against the Murdering, Thieving Hordes of Peasants' (May 1525) — urging princes to 'stab, slay, kill' the rebels mercilessly
choices: 'Against the Murdering, Thieving Hordes of Peasants' (May 1525) — urging princes to 'stab, slay, kill' the rebels mercilessly
'In Defense of the Wretched Peasants' (May 1525) — calling on princes to grant the Twelve Articles by Christian charity
'Concerning the Two Kingdoms' (May 1525) — refusing comment on temporal politics as outside the gospel's scope
'A Lament for the Slain' (May 1525) — mourning the peasant dead while regretfully accepting their need for suppression
context: Luther's 'Against the Murdering, Thieving Hordes' is among the most controversial documents of the Reformation. He had urged moderation earlier, but the peasant atrocities at Weinsberg (April 1525) hardened him. The text helped lose the peasant cause but secured princely support for the Reformation. The 'two kingdoms' distinction — secular sword distinct from spiritual gospel — was Luther's framework.

question: From October 1-3, 1529, at Marburg Castle, Philip of Hesse — a Protestant prince hoping to unite the Reformation against Catholic powers — sponsored a meeting between Luther, Zwingli, and other reformers. They agreed on 14 of 15 articles of faith. They could not agree on the 15th, regarding the Eucharist. Luther reportedly wrote on the table in chalk a Latin phrase from Christ's institution. What did he write?
answer: 'Hoc est corpus meum' — 'This is my body' — insisting on the literal meaning against Zwingli's symbolic reading
choices: 'Hoc est corpus meum' — 'This is my body' — insisting on the literal meaning against Zwingli's symbolic reading
'Sola fide' — 'By faith alone' — insisting on justification as the foundation of all sacramental theology
'Caro non prodest' — 'The flesh profits nothing' — Zwingli's countertext that Luther reportedly used to mock him
'Tu es Petrus' — 'You are Peter' — the Catholic papal text that Luther mockingly applied to Zwingli's claim
context: Luther insisted on the literal interpretation of 'Hoc est corpus meum' — 'this IS my body.' Zwingli insisted 'est' meant 'signifies.' Without agreement on Eucharist, the Protestant front was permanently divided. Marburg's failure was a structural disaster — the Reformation produced Lutheran, Reformed, and Anabaptist movements that fought each other as fiercely as they fought Rome.

question: John Knox (c. 1514-1572) founded Scottish Presbyterianism — Calvin's most fiery disciple. Originally a Catholic priest, he converted in the 1540s, served as a Marian galley slave (1547-1549), and lived in Geneva (1556-1558) absorbing Calvin's theology. Returning to Scotland in 1559, he led the Reformation. What was his most famous polemical work, directed against whom?
answer: The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558) — against female rulers Mary Tudor and Mary Stuart
choices: The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558) — against female rulers Mary Tudor and Mary Stuart
The Scots Confession (1560) — Scotland's first Reformed confession, which Knox principally drafted with five others
The Book of Discipline (1561) — establishing Presbyterian church governance throughout Scotland by parish and synod
The History of the Reformation in Scotland — published posthumously, covering events from Hamilton's martyrdom to 1567
context: The First Blast (1558) attacked female rule generally and Catholic queens Mary I of England and Mary of Guise of Scotland specifically. The title meant 'monstrous regiment' as 'unnatural rule.' Awkwardly, Elizabeth I came to the throne the same year — and never forgave Knox the polemic. His confrontations with Mary Queen of Scots after 1561 became legendary.

question: In January 1604, at the Hampton Court Conference after James VI of Scotland became James I of England, the Puritan John Reynolds proposed a new authorized Bible. James approved; the work went to 47 scholars in six companies at Oxford, Cambridge, and Westminster. They began work in 1607 and completed in 1611. What was the principal aim, and what made the King James distinctive?
answer: An authorized text for public worship — readable aloud, dignified, drawing heavily on Tyndale (NT) and the Geneva (OT)
choices: An authorized text for public worship — readable aloud, dignified, drawing heavily on Tyndale (NT) and the Geneva (OT)
A scholarly text from original languages — replacing the Latin Vulgate for academic theological study primarily
A simple text for the common people — written in deliberately plain colloquial English of the early 17th century
A Puritan text — replacing the Bishops' Bible favored by the Anglican establishment with a Reformed alternative
context: The King James Version (or Authorized Version, AV) shaped English religious and literary language for 350+ years. About 75% of its NT comes from Tyndale; its phrasings ('through a glass darkly,' 'the powers that be,' 'a thorn in the flesh') saturate English usage. Modern critical editions correct its textual base; for literary power and historical influence it remains unmatched in English religious translation.

question: In 1630, a much larger Puritan migration arrived in New England — about 700 settlers on 11 ships, led by John Winthrop. Unlike the earlier Pilgrim Separatists, the Massachusetts Bay Puritans regarded themselves as still part of the Church of England, intending to establish a model 'pure' church. On board the Arbella in 1630, Winthrop gave a famous sermon. What was its central image?
answer: 'A city upon a hill' — Matthew 5:14 applied to the colony as a Christian model the eyes of the world would watch
choices: 'A city upon a hill' — Matthew 5:14 applied to the colony as a Christian model the eyes of the world would watch
'A burning bush' — Exodus 3 applied to the colony as a beacon of Reformation faith in the wilderness
'A new Jerusalem' — Revelation 21 applied to the colony as the eschatological community fulfilling prophecy
'A righteous remnant' — Isaiah 10 applied to the colony as the survivors of the Old England Antichrist persecution
context: Winthrop's 'Model of Christian Charity' delivered the 'city upon a hill' phrase later quoted by John F. Kennedy and Ronald Reagan. The Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630) grew rapidly; by 1640 about 20,000 Puritans had crossed the Atlantic. The colony established Congregationalist churches, town meeting governance, Harvard College (1636), and Salem (where the witch trials occurred in 1692).

question: On March 25, 1807, the British Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act, ending British participation in the Atlantic slave trade. The principal architect of the political campaign — sustained over twenty years (his first bill was 1789) — was an evangelical Anglican MP and friend of William Pitt the Younger. He was supported by a Christian network known as the Clapham Sect. Who was he?
answer: William Wilberforce — whose evangelical conversion in 1785 turned him to abolitionism and 'reformation of manners'
choices: William Wilberforce — whose evangelical conversion in 1785 turned him to abolitionism and 'reformation of manners'
Lord Mansfield — Chief Justice whose 1772 Somerset v. Stewart ruling effectively ended slavery in England itself
John Newton — former slave-ship captain turned Anglican curate who wrote 'Amazing Grace' (1779) on his conversion
Granville Sharp — abolitionist lawyer who brought the Somerset case and helped Wilberforce on the parliamentary campaign
context: Wilberforce's twenty-year campaign for abolition is one of the great moral political victories of modern history. The Slave Trade Act 1807 ended British trade; the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 (passed three days before Wilberforce's death) emancipated slaves throughout the British Empire. The Clapham Sect — evangelical Anglicans pooling effort across causes — pioneered many techniques of modern political activism.

question: Around 1820, a 14-year-old upstate New York farm boy named Joseph Smith Jr. (1805-1844) — caught up in the religious revivals of the 'Burned-Over District' and confused by competing claims of denominations — went into a grove of trees on his family's farm near Manchester, NY, to pray about which church to join. He later reported a vision. What did he claim?
answer: The Father and the Son appeared to him in pillars of light; he was told to join none of the existing churches
choices: The Father and the Son appeared to him in pillars of light; he was told to join none of the existing churches
An angel named Moroni appeared to him with golden plates; this was actually three years later in September 1823
He saw the resurrected Christ standing on a stone altar offering him a new testament for the American continent
He received the gift of tongues and began prophesying in Hebrew; this was actually witnessed by his father Joseph Sr.
context: Smith's 'First Vision' (recounted in 1832, 1835, 1838, and 1842 with various details) became foundational for Mormonism. Three years later (September 21, 1823), Smith reported the angel Moroni appearing and directing him to golden plates containing the Book of Mormon, which he claimed to translate and publish in 1830. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) considers Smith its founding prophet.

question: After Joseph Smith Jr.'s 1844 lynching at Carthage, Illinois, the Latter-day Saints were left fractured and embattled. The largest faction followed Brigham Young (1801-1877), president of the Quorum of the Twelve, who led the Mormons west across the plains in one of the largest religious migrations in American history. On July 24, 1847, Young arrived in the Great Salt Lake Valley with the vanguard company. What did he reportedly say?
answer: 'This is the place' — directing the settlement of what became Salt Lake City in then-Mexican territory
choices: 'This is the place' — directing the settlement of what became Salt Lake City in then-Mexican territory
'The desert shall blossom as the rose' — quoting Isaiah 35:1 as commission for irrigation and cultivation
'Here we build the Temple' — pointing to the site of the future Salt Lake Temple (built 1853-1893)
'We are Israel come home' — declaring the Salt Lake basin a new promised land for the Saints
context: Young's 'This is the place' (later commemorated in This Is The Place Heritage Park in Salt Lake City) marked the founding of Mormon Utah. The territory was Mexican until the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) made it American. Young served as territorial governor 1850-1857; succeeded as church president by John Taylor in 1880. The polygamy controversy with the federal government dominated late 19th-century Utah politics.

question: On October 11, 1962, Pope John XXIII opened the Second Vatican Council, having called it in January 1959 to widespread surprise (he had been elected as a transitional 'caretaker' pope at age 76). Four sessions ran from 1962 through December 1965 (Paul VI succeeded John XXIII in 1963). The council produced 16 documents reshaping Catholic life. What was John XXIII's word for the council's purpose?
answer: Aggiornamento — 'bringing up to date' — opening the church to dialogue with the modern world
choices: Aggiornamento — 'bringing up to date' — opening the church to dialogue with the modern world
Anathema — 'curse' — condemning modernist heresies that had infiltrated the church since Vatican I
Anamnesis — 'remembering' — restoring liturgical and patristic practices that had been forgotten
Acclamatio — 'acclamation' — emphasizing lay involvement in the assembly of the Eucharistic liturgy
context: Vatican II's major documents — Lumen Gentium (the church), Dei Verbum (revelation), Sacrosanctum Concilium (liturgy), Gaudium et Spes (the church in the modern world), Nostra Aetate (non-Christian religions), Dignitatis Humanae (religious freedom) — reshaped Catholic life. The Mass moved to vernacular languages; relations with other Christians and non-Christians transformed.

question: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906-1945) was a German Lutheran pastor, theologian, and resistance figure. After 1933 he opposed the Nazi co-optation of the German church, helping found the Confessing Church (Barmen Declaration, 1934). He ran an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde. In 1939 he chose to return from safety in New York to Germany. He participated in the resistance and the July 20, 1944 assassination plot against Hitler. What was his fate?
answer: Arrested April 1943; hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp April 9, 1945 — two weeks before liberation
choices: Arrested April 1943; hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp April 9, 1945 — two weeks before liberation
Escaped to Switzerland in October 1944 after the failed plot; spent the post-war decade writing prison letters
Survived the war in hiding; emigrated to America in 1946 and taught at Union Theological Seminary until 1955
Captured at the Swiss border January 1945; held in Berlin until killed in the Soviet artillery shelling of April 1945
context: Bonhoeffer was hanged at Flossenbürg by special SS order on Hitler's direct command, April 9, 1945 — the camp was liberated by US forces April 23. His Letters and Papers from Prison (published 1951) and The Cost of Discipleship (1937) became Christian classics. His 'religionless Christianity' phrase from prison provoked decades of theological debate. The 1944 plot's failure cost him his life.

question: C. S. Lewis (1898-1963), Oxford literary scholar, described his 1929 acceptance of theism as 'the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.' Two years later (September 1931), on a long conversation in the Magdalen College grounds with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson, his final conversion to Christianity occurred. The next morning he experienced something distinctive. What was it?
answer: Riding on his brother Warnie's motorcycle sidecar to Whipsnade Zoo, he arrived believing what he had not believed when they set out
choices: Riding on his brother Warnie's motorcycle sidecar to Whipsnade Zoo, he arrived believing what he had not believed when they set out
Writing The Pilgrim's Regress in a single weekend in his Magdalen College rooms recounting his entire spiritual journey
Receiving Confirmation from the Anglican bishop of Oxford in a private ceremony arranged by his college chaplain
Preaching his first sermon at the Magdalen College chapel on the text 'Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief'
context: Lewis's motorcycle-to-the-zoo conversion (September 28, 1931) is recounted in Surprised by Joy. He went on to become the most influential lay Christian writer of the 20th century in English — Mere Christianity (1952), The Screwtape Letters (1942), the Chronicles of Narnia (1950-1956), The Problem of Pain (1940). His friend Tolkien remained Catholic; Lewis returned to the Anglican Church of his Belfast childhood.

question: J. R. R. Tolkien (1892-1973), Oxford philologist and friend of C. S. Lewis, was a devout Catholic whose religious faith infuses his fictional creation Middle-earth without ever appearing explicitly. The Lord of the Rings (published 1954-1955) was, he wrote in a letter, 'a fundamentally religious and Catholic work; unconsciously so at first, but consciously in the revision.' What specifically Catholic element did Tolkien attribute his deepest source to?
answer: The Eucharist — specifically the Blessed Sacrament as the inspiration for the lembas wayfaring bread of the Elves
choices: The Eucharist — specifically the Blessed Sacrament as the inspiration for the lembas wayfaring bread of the Elves
The Rosary — the prayer he said daily and which structures the chapter rhythms of the Lord of the Rings
The Mass — specifically the Latin Tridentine Mass which he attended and refused to abandon after Vatican II
The papacy — the papal infallibility of 1870 specifically inspired the resistance to Sauron's One Ring
context: Tolkien wrote in Letter 213 (1958): 'I am a Christian (which can be deduced from my stories), and in fact a Roman Catholic.' Letter 250 (1963) cited the Blessed Sacrament. The 'three things that Christianity has done for me' he listed elsewhere as the Blessed Sacrament, the Mass, the Holy Mother. He was instrumental in C. S. Lewis's 1931 conversion to Christianity; they remained close friends until Tolkien's distress at Lewis's marriage in 1956.

question: Reformed (Calvinist) theology was systematized in response to Arminian challenges at the Synod of Dort (1618-1619). The synod's findings were later organized in the English-speaking world by the acronym TULIP. The 'T' stands for Total Depravity. What does this doctrine actually teach?
answer: Every aspect of human nature is corrupted by sin; humans cannot will spiritual good without God's prior grace
choices: Every aspect of human nature is corrupted by sin; humans cannot will spiritual good without God's prior grace
Every human action is as wicked as it could possibly be; humans are unable to perform any genuine moral good
All humans are equally and absolutely depraved; no distinction in degrees of sin can be made among persons
The total depraved population of humanity outnumbers the elect by an unknown but very large fixed ratio
context: Total depravity does NOT teach humans are as bad as they could be — only that no part of fallen human nature is untouched by sin's corruption. The doctrine is sometimes called 'total inability' to clarify: humans cannot, on their own, turn to God. Critics charge it makes God responsible for choosing not to save those he could have. Defenders charge alternatives make salvation depend partly on human will, denying salvation by grace alone.

question: Four major athletic festivals — the Panhellenic Games — bound the Greek world together. Each was held in honor of a god, on a regular cycle, with sacred truces declared. What were the four games, their gods, and their cycles?
answer: Olympic (Zeus, Olympia, every 4 years); Pythian (Apollo, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Poseidon, Corinth, every 2 years); Nemean (Zeus, Nemea, every 2 years)
choices: Olympic (Zeus, Olympia, every 4 years); Pythian (Apollo, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Poseidon, Corinth, every 2 years); Nemean (Zeus, Nemea, every 2 years)
Olympic (Zeus, Athens, every 4 years); Pythian (Athena, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Apollo, Corinth, every 2 years); Heraion (Hera, Argos, every 2 years)
Olympic (Apollo, Olympia, every 5 years); Pythian (Zeus, Delphi, every 5 years); Isthmian (Hera, Corinth, every 3 years); Nemean (Athena, Nemea, every 3 years)
Olympic (Aphrodite, Olympia, every 4 years); Pythian (Hermes, Delphi, every 4 years); Isthmian (Dionysus, Corinth, every 2 years); Nemean (Demeter, Nemea, every 2 years)
context: The Panhellenic Games schedule was staggered so that two of the four occurred every year. The Olympic Games (founded traditionally 776 BC, the year 1 of Greek dating) were the most prestigious. Victors received olive wreaths (or laurel at Pythian, pine at Isthmian, wild celery at Nemean) — material wealth came from their home cities afterward. The sacred truce (ekecheiria) protected athletes and spectators from war.

question: After the gods created the world from Ymir's body, they walked along the shore of the new world and found two pieces of driftwood — an ash log and an elm log (per the standard version). They breathed life and consciousness into them, creating the first humans. What were the first humans' names?
answer: Ask (ash) and Embla (elm) — the first man and woman; ancestors of all humanity in Norse mythology
choices: Ask (ash) and Embla (elm) — the first man and woman; ancestors of all humanity in Norse mythology
Buri and Bestla — actually a god and a giantess, the grandparents of Odin from earlier in cosmogony
Lif and Lifthrasir — actually the two humans who survive Ragnarok hidden in Yggdrasil, not the first humans
Bor and Borr — variant names of Odin's father; not the first humans but rather the proto-gods
context: Ask (ash tree) and Embla (elm) were given three gifts by three gods: Odin gave breath/spirit (önd), Hoenir (or Vili) gave consciousness/sense, Lóðurr (or Ve) gave warmth/blood. The myth gave Norse humanity a wooden origin — appropriate to a culture so dependent on forests. Compare Hesiod's Pandora (clay) and Genesis's Adam (clay) — the Norse choice of wood is distinctive.

question: The Germanic peoples had a runic alphabet known as the Futhark (named for its first six letters: f, u, þ, a, r, k). The earliest version — Elder Futhark — had how many letters? And what replaced it later?
answer: 24 letters in Elder Futhark (c. 150-800 AD); replaced by 16-letter Younger Futhark (c. 800-1100 AD) used in Viking Age
choices: 24 letters in Elder Futhark (c. 150-800 AD); replaced by 16-letter Younger Futhark (c. 800-1100 AD) used in Viking Age
16 letters in Elder Futhark; expanded to 33 letters in Anglo-Saxon Futhorc, used into the late Middle Ages
33 letters in Elder Futhark; simplified to 16 in Viking-age Younger Futhark for ease of carving on weapons
12 letters in Elder Futhark; doubled to 24 in Younger Futhark for the more elaborate Viking-age inscriptions
context: Elder Futhark (24 runes) → Younger Futhark (16 runes) in Scandinavia (Viking-age). Anglo-Saxon Futhorc (29-33 runes) developed separately in England. Runes were used for inscriptions on stone (runestones), wood, bone, metal — not for everyday writing. They had names (Fehu = cattle/wealth; Uruz = aurochs; Thurisaz = giant; etc.) with phonetic and symbolic meaning. Used into early modern Iceland for inscriptions; survived in Sweden's Dalecarlian runes into the 20th century.

question: Iceland was settled in 874 AD by the Norwegian chieftain Ingólfur Arnarson. Many of the settlers were chieftains fleeing the centralization of power under King Harald Fairhair of Norway. The settlement period (Landnámsöld) lasted from 874 to about 930. What kind of government did the early Icelanders establish?
answer: The Althing in 930 AD — assembly of free men meeting annually at Thingvellir — perhaps the oldest extant parliament
choices: The Althing in 930 AD — assembly of free men meeting annually at Thingvellir — perhaps the oldest extant parliament
A kingdom under Ingólfur's descendants — the Icelanders established a royal line that endured until 1262
A theocracy under the goði (chieftain-priests) — religion and government were inseparable in early Icelandic society
An anarchic federation — no central institutions developed until Norway annexed the island in 1262 AD
context: The Althing — founded 930 at Thingvellir (Þingvellir, 'Assembly Plains') — is the oldest continuously functioning parliament in the world (with some interruptions). It met annually for two weeks in June, with cases heard, laws recited, news exchanged. The Lawspeaker (lögsögumaður) memorized the laws and recited them. Iceland's medieval Commonwealth (930-1262) operated without a king — a unique European experiment that ended when civil wars led to Norwegian rule.

question: At the Althing in the year 1000 AD (June 23, by traditional dating), Iceland made a decision unique among European Christianizations. The country had been divided between pagans and Christians; civil war was threatened. The decision was put to one man — the Lawspeaker Thorgeir Ljósvetningagoði (who was himself a pagan). He went under a cloak for a day and a night without speaking. What did he announce?
answer: All Icelanders should be baptized Christian — but private pagan practice was allowed for the time being
choices: All Icelanders should be baptized Christian — but private pagan practice was allowed for the time being
All Icelanders should remain pagan — Christianity was rejected at the assembly by a single binding vote
All Icelanders should divide by district — northern districts pagan, southern districts Christian forever
All Icelanders should consult Norway — the king was to decide for them in a binding manner
context: Thorgeir's compromise — Christianity as official religion, with private pagan practice allowed — kept the peace. Within a generation, pagan practice faded. The conversion was relatively peaceful, in striking contrast to the Christianizations of Norway (forcible under Olaf Tryggvason and Olaf Haraldsson), Sweden (slow, resistant), and Saxony (Charlemagne's massacre at Verden). Thingvellir is where the conversion was decided.

question: On June 8, 793 AD, a fleet of Norse longships appeared off the holy island of Lindisfarne, the great monastery off the coast of Northumbria in northern England. They sacked the monastery, killing monks and seizing treasures. This is traditionally taken as the start of what era?
answer: The Viking Age (c. 793-1066) — three centuries of Norse expansion, raiding, trading, settlement across Europe and beyond
choices: The Viking Age (c. 793-1066) — three centuries of Norse expansion, raiding, trading, settlement across Europe and beyond
The Heptarchy — actually the seven Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of England, predating the Vikings by centuries
The Christianization of Scandinavia — actually a much later event, starting around 960 AD with Harald Bluetooth
The Carolingian Renaissance — actually Charlemagne's cultural revival, happening on the Continent during this period
context: Lindisfarne marks the conventional start of the Viking Age. The shock was enormous — the great churchman Alcuin (in Charlemagne's court) wrote that 'such a horror had never before appeared in Britain.' The Vikings would raid, trade, and settle for three centuries — Norse settlements in Iceland, Greenland (985), Vinland (c. 1000), the Danelaw in England, Normandy in France, Rus in Russia, the Varangian Guard in Constantinople.

question: The most famous pagan Norse temple was at Uppsala in Sweden. Adam of Bremen (writing c. 1075) described the great festival held there every nine years. What did Adam claim happened at these festivals?
answer: Nine of every kind of male animal were sacrificed, including humans; bodies hung in the sacred grove beside the temple
choices: Nine of every kind of male animal were sacrificed, including humans; bodies hung in the sacred grove beside the temple
Only flower offerings — Uppsala was a peaceful sanctuary contrasting with the warlike practices of southern Vikings
Only gold tribute — no living sacrifices; the temple was richly decorated but pacifist in its religious approach
Only the recitation of poems — Uppsala's nine-year ritual was a poetic festival rather than a sacrificial one
context: Adam of Bremen described 72 victims (nine of each of eight kinds of male animal, plus humans) hung in the sacred grove. Modern scholarship debates whether Adam was accurate — he was a hostile Christian source — but the general pattern of Germanic sacrifice (blot) is well-attested. The pagan temple at Uppsala was destroyed when Sweden converted to Christianity in the late 11th century; modern Uppsala Cathedral stands near the original site.

question: The Norse word for sacrificial worship was 'blót' (related to English 'blood'). Blót involved sacrificing animals (sometimes humans) to the gods. What was the basic structure of a blót ritual?
answer: Animals slaughtered with the blood sprinkled on the altar and the participants; meat eaten communally with the gods present
choices: Animals slaughtered with the blood sprinkled on the altar and the participants; meat eaten communally with the gods present
Animals abandoned alive in sacred groves; the gods would either accept them (they vanished) or reject them (they survived)
Animals burned entirely in offering to the gods; no part was eaten by humans, with the smoke being the divine portion
Animals presented at the temple but not killed; only after a year's keeping could the animals be ritually slaughtered
context: Blót shared the basic structure of Greek and Roman sacrifice: the animal was dedicated, killed, the blood used for ritual purposes, the meat cooked and eaten communally with the divine presence assumed. This combined religion and communal feasting — the social and religious functions of sacrifice were inseparable. The transition to Christianity ended public blót but private practices continued in some forms.

question: The volva (plural völur) — Norse seeress, female practitioner of seidr — had a distinctive social and religious role. She wandered between farms, was given hospitality, prophesied for her hosts, and could mediate with the spirit world. What did the volva wear and carry?
answer: A cloak of blue or black; a hood; a staff (vǫlr — same root as her name); often catskin gloves
choices: A cloak of blue or black; a hood; a staff (vǫlr — same root as her name); often catskin gloves
A robe of crimson silk; a golden crown; a sword and shield; a small portable altar of bronze
A linen veil; a wreath of mistletoe; a chalice and a runic tablet; sandals of woven hemp
A long mantle of bear-fur; a copper diadem; nothing else — the volva traveled with no implements of her trade
context: Eiríks saga rauða (Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 4) describes a volva in detail visiting a farmstead in Greenland. She wore a hooded blue cloak, glass beads, catskin gloves with white fur inside, a hammer-shaped pouch with charms, a staff. She sat on a special platform and entered trance for prophecy. The description has helped scholars understand volva practice as an actual social institution, not just literary motif.

question: Norse warrior bands included some who entered a battle-frenzy state — fighting with extraordinary ferocity, ignoring wounds, perhaps believing themselves to embody animal spirits. The Old Norse term for these warriors is the source of the English word 'berserk.' What did the name mean?
answer: Berserkr — perhaps 'bear-shirt' (wearing bear-hide) or 'bare-shirt' (fighting without armor); etymological debate continues
choices: Berserkr — perhaps 'bear-shirt' (wearing bear-hide) or 'bare-shirt' (fighting without armor); etymological debate continues
Berserkr — 'bare-blade' — referring to warriors who fought without sheathed weapons in battle frenzy
Berserkr — 'big-arm' — referring to warriors of exceptional physical size and strength alone
Berserkr — 'broad-shield' — referring to the distinctive large round shields these warriors carried
context: Berserkr's etymology is debated but probably 'bear-shirt' (warriors wearing bear-hides) or possibly 'bare-shirt' (without armor). Related: ulfheðnar ('wolf-coats'), wearing wolf-hides. These warriors were sometimes Odin's special followers, perhaps a kind of religious brotherhood. Modern theories about psychoactive substances (mushrooms, alcohol) inducing the frenzy state are speculative. The phenomenon was real — berserker laws prohibited their excesses in Iceland after Christianization.

question: Vikings of high status were sometimes buried in ships — vessels covered with earth as great burial mounds. The most famous such ships have been excavated in modern times in Norway. Which two ship burials provided the best-preserved evidence?
answer: Oseberg (c. 834 AD, contained two female bodies and rich grave goods) and Gokstad (c. 900 AD, contained a chieftain)
